title: A 10-Minute Morning Yoga Routine You Can Do Without Leaving Your Bed
excerpt: From bridge pose to spinal twists, experts say a brief stretch sequence in bed can reduce stiffness, boost energy, and set a positive tone for the day.
body:
• A 10-minute morning yoga routine performed in bed can improve flexibility, reduce stiffness, and boost energy without requiring a mat or studio.
  • Experts recommend poses like bridge, spinal twists, and forward folds that target large muscle groups left tight after sleep.
  • Research links brief daily yoga sessions to lower stress, better posture, and improved mental clarity throughout the day.

The alarm sounds. Your body feels stiff, your lower back aches from hours in the fetal position, and the thought of a full workout feels unrealistic. But what if the most effective thing you could do for your body required nothing more than staying in bed for 10 extra minutes?

A growing body of evidence — and a wave of expert-backed routines from yoga instructors and movement therapists — suggests that a short morning yoga practice performed on your mattress can deliver meaningful physical and mental benefits, no gym membership required.

Why Morning Yoga Works

After a night of sleep, the body's muscles are shortened and stiff, particularly in the hips, hamstrings, and spine. A brief yoga sequence targets these areas, drawing blood flow to large muscle groups and lubricating joints that stiffen overnight.

"Even 10 minutes of yoga a day has been shown to help reduce stress, improve mobility and flexibility, improve your posture, and boost energy and mental clarity," says Kelly Smith, a yoga and meditation teacher and founder of Yoga For You. "It will also help reduce the discomfort in the upper body most people have if they work desk jobs."

Molly Schenck, a registered somatic movement educator and certified yoga teacher, adds that morning movement is as much mental as physical. "Moving first thing in the morning is a great way to set an intention for your day," Schenck says. "It not only wakes the body but allows you to focus on what you want to accomplish."

A Sequence You Can Do on Your Mattress

Several expert-designed routines — including sequences from Yoga Journal and certified instructors — follow a similar structure: start lying down, move through gentle mobilisations, and finish seated. Here is a consolidated 10-minute flow based on widely recommended poses.

Full-body stretch (1 minute): Lie flat, reach your arms overhead and your feet away from you, stretching from head to toe. Release and repeat.

Bridge pose (1 minute): Bend your knees, plant your feet on the bed, and press through your hands and feet to lift your hips. This engages the glutes and hamstrings while opening the chest.

Knees to chest (1 minute): Draw both knees toward your chest and wrap your arms around your shins, gently rocking side to side to massage the lower back.

Supine spinal twist (2 minutes): Cross one knee over your body toward the opposite side while keeping your shoulder grounded. Hold for a minute on each side. This improves spinal mobility and releases lower back tension.

Figure 4 stretch (2 minutes): Cross one ankle over the opposite knee and draw the bottom knee toward your chest. This opens tight hips — a common problem for those who sit at desks all day. Repeat on both sides.

"Let it be easy, and don't overthink it. You will absolutely feel better even after a few minutes of morning yoga."

— Kelly Smith, yoga and meditation teacher

Seated side stretch (1 minute): Sit cross-legged, reach your arms overhead, interlace your fingers, and lean to each side. This lengthens the muscles along the ribcage and spine.

Seated forward fold (1 minute): Extend your legs and fold forward from the hips, rounding your back and releasing your neck. Targets hamstrings, calves, and the posterior chain.

Seated breathing (1 minute): Close your eyes, exhale through your lips, inhale through your nose. Five to ten cycles of controlled breath to centre yourself before starting the day.

What the Research Says

A study published in the International Journal of Yoga found that regular yoga practice improves flexibility, balance, and muscular strength. Separate research in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology showed that yoga reduces cortisol levels — the hormone associated with stress — particularly when practised in the morning.

Austin Martinez, vice president of training at StretchLab, notes that focusing on larger muscle groups first maximises the benefits of a short session. "Focusing on the hamstrings, quadriceps, glutes, erector spinae, and the chest area would be best," he says, since these draw the most blood flow and circulation.

Building the Habit

Experts say consistency matters more than duration. Schenck recommends preparing the night before — setting out a journal, candle, or intention — and practising in pyjamas to remove barriers. "Make it as easy as possible to roll out of bed and into movement," she advises.

For diaspora Indians juggling long commutes and high-pressure careers, a bed-based routine offers a practical bridge to the wellness traditions many grew up with. No Sanskrit required — just 10 minutes and a willingness to stretch.
